extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in disinformation and information operations
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize methods, mechanisms, and frameworks used to produce, amplify, and counter disinformation online, including technical, psychological, economic, and policy dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet manipulation purposes/effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation may be used to steer public opinion, polarise citizens, circulate conspiracy theories, and silence political dissidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explicitly lists these as principal aims of internet manipulation; it also notes manipulation can be done for profit (to harm corporate or political adversaries and improve brand reputation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational propaganda (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation for propaganda purposes with the help of data analysis and internet bots in social media is called computational propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames a category of activity combining automated tools and analytics to amplify political messaging; used as a label for coordinated, technical propaganda efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four main methods of seeding disinformation online
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show four main methods of seeding disinformation online: selective censorship; manipulation of search rankings; hacking and releasing; directly sharing disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four methods are presented as primary vectors by which false or harmful information is initially placed into information ecosystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI swarms as an emerging threat
rubrics_metrics.description: AI technology could enable groups of AI programs, known as 'AI swarms,' to autonomously coordinate to manipulate democratic discourse by maintaining persistent fake identities and mimicking human social dynamics over extended periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights an anticipated technical capability that would allow long-term, scalable impersonation and social interaction to influence publics without human operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of online advertising technologies (amplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation is amplified online due to malpractice concerning online advertising, especially the machine-to-machine interactions of real-time bidding systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites real-time bidding and programmatic ad systems as technical/amplification pathways where ad tech facilitates spreading disinformation via automated buying/selling of placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization and financial incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Online advertising technologies have been used to amplify disinformation due to the financial incentives and monetization of user-generated content and fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary incentives (ad revenue, monetizable engagement) are identified as drivers encouraging producers/distributors of disinformation to scale and persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lax oversight and dark money in political advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The lax oversight over the online advertising market can be used to amplify disinformation, including the use of dark money used for political advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and regulatory weaknesses (poor oversight, opaque funding) are listed as systemic vulnerabilities enabling concealed or unaccountable disinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective enforcement of internet censorship and net neutrality as manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet manipulation is sometimes also used to describe the selective enforcement of Internet censorship or selective violations of net neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expands the notion of manipulation beyond content seeding to include structural/network-level policies or enforcement decisions that shape information flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics and techniques of disinformation (catalogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad set of tactics used in disinformation: astroturfing, Big Lie, black propaganda, circular reporting, clickbait, conspiracy theory, deepfake, doublespeak, doxxing, fear uncertainty and doubt, firehose of falsehood, forgery as covert operation, gaslighting, historical negationism, hoax, misinformation tools such as fake news websites, smear campaigns, spin, and many others listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides an extensive taxonomy of tactics and deceptive techniques—useful for classification and for recognizing operational patterns in campaigns. (The navbox lists many individual items worth mapping to detection/mitigation strategies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and social mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms by which disinformation spreads and persuades include cognitive bias, illusory truth effect, social engineering, echo chambers, emotional appeals (appeal to fear, appeal to emotion), framing, and other psychological vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms explain why audiences accept and retransmit false claims; they are key criteria when evaluating the likely impact of a piece of content or an intervention's design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of disinformation (formats/channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation can take forms such as advertising, propaganda, fake news, public relations, spin, tabloid journalism, user-generated content, state media, streaming media, social media posts, and influencer content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying the form helps tailor response strategies (e.g., regulation of political ads vs. debunking viral social posts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification channels and actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Channels and actors that amplify disinformation include social bots, social networking services, programmatic advertising, fake news websites, influencers, state actors, and coordinated networks (e.g., botnets or troll farms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links actor types and technical channels to amplification dynamics—useful when assessing source credibility, scale, and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic and policy frameworks for understanding/countering disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frameworks and standards referenced include the DMMI Matrix (DMMI), the ABC disinformation framework, the ABCDE Framework (Carnegie), NATO's 'DISARM' defence standards, and the Strengthened Code of Practice on Disinformation (European Commission, 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as conceptual tools and policy-oriented standards to classify, assess risk, guide industry/regulator responses, and coordinate countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for countering disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Countering methods listed include academic research, critical thinking/digital literacy/media literacy/health literacy/information literacy/science communication, watchdog journalism, fact-checking, transparency measures, and platform/content-moderation interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article groups practical and normative responses spanning education, journalism, platform policy, and regulatory action; these are the primary response categories for practitioners and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical findings relevant to impact assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Research findings cited (e.g., that false news spreads more quickly than true news; bots' role in fighting opposition) provide empirical bases for evaluating how and why disinformation affects attitudes and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a prescriptive rubric, these empirical results are offered as evidence to prioritize interventions, assess risk, and evaluate the likely reach and persistence of disinformation campaigns.
